# Media and the Browser

Receiving bytes is not the same as hearing sound or seeing a picture.

The relay says objects are arriving. The player remains black. That can happen without any transport bug: a media application needs more information than the payload bytes alone.

## The format supplies meaning

A receiver needs to know which track contains audio, which codec was used, how to configure the decoder, and when to present each decoded frame. The media format provides the agreement between publisher and receiver.

MOQT is deliberately content agnostic. It does not require every application to use one codec or interpret one object as one video frame. Two endpoints can speak the same transport and still disagree about what its payload means.

## A catalog describes the choices

In the moq.dev ecosystem, **hang** supplies a media catalog and frame packaging above moq-lite. The catalog describes media renditions and their decoder configuration. This lets a player discover available choices instead of guessing from track names.

A lecture might offer one audio track and several video renditions. The player must select a rendition it can decode and afford to receive. “Highest resolution” is not necessarily the right initial choice on an unknown connection.

For example, a video rendition's metadata might describe H.264 pictures at 1280 × 720 pixels. The codec identifier tells the receiver which decoder it needs; the dimensions describe the encoded pictures; decoder initialization data supplies codec-specific setup. The container field tells the receiver how to separate timing information from encoded media bytes.

In hang, the player first reads the `catalog.json` track, chooses a supported rendition, subscribes to its media track, parses the declared container, and passes encoded chunks to the decoder. These are [hang conventions](https://doc.moq.dev/concept/hang), not requirements imposed by MOQT on every application.

Catalogs can change during a publication. A player needs to handle a track appearing, disappearing, or becoming unusable. Treat metadata as part of the live system rather than a permanent fact learned only at startup.

## Keyframes and dependencies

Many video frames describe changes from other pictures. A **keyframe**, in the simple model used here, supplies a fresh decoding starting point. Later predicted frames depend on the decoder having the appropriate reference pictures.

That is why our example aligns group boundaries with independent video sequences. Arbitrarily cutting a byte stream every second does not necessarily produce safe join points. The encoder and packager must agree on the boundary.

Switching video quality has the same concern. A low-resolution frame and a high-resolution frame are not automatically interchangeable decoder state. Switch at a valid point with the correct configuration for the new rendition.

## WebCodecs handles codec work

WebCodecs exposes low-level encoding and decoding interfaces. It can turn encoded chunks into decoded frames, but it does not implement a complete MoQ player. The application still needs transport, demultiplexing or parsing, buffering, synchronization, and rendering.

A decoder configuration must be supported on the actual device. Detect support rather than assuming that an API being present means every codec, profile, resolution, or acceleration path is available.

For video, the basic WebCodecs sequence is to check a configuration with `VideoDecoder.isConfigSupported()`, apply it with `configure()`, and submit encoded chunks with `decode()`. Decoded pictures arrive through an output callback as `VideoFrame` objects. That callback does not automatically display them: the player must schedule and render them.

Call `VideoFrame.close()` when a frame is no longer needed. Keeping frames until garbage collection can retain scarce decoder resources and stall decoding. Bound the application's queues as well: a slow renderer must not turn every incoming picture into more pending work. See the [WebCodecs decoder interface](https://www.w3.org/TR/webcodecs/#videodecoder-interface) and [resource memory model](https://www.w3.org/TR/webcodecs/#raw-media-memory-model).

## Timestamps are not arrival times

Packets take variable amounts of time to travel. This variation in delivery timing is called **jitter**. If a player displays each frame immediately upon arrival, uneven network timing becomes uneven presentation. Media timestamps let it schedule content according to the intended timeline.

Consider three frames in a simplified playback timeline. All numbers below are milliseconds; the media clock and receiver clock have different origins.

| Frame | Media timestamp | Arrival on receiver clock | Planned display on receiver clock |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| A | 0 | 100 | 160 |
| B | 33 | 145 | 193 |
| C | 67 | 150 | 227 |

The player chooses to display media time zero at receiver time 160. Adding each media timestamp to that anchor preserves the intended spacing, even though arrivals are uneven. The initial wait leaves room for some network variation. If B instead arrives at receiver time 205, it misses its planned display time; the player needs a late-frame policy, such as skipping it or moving playback later.

This is an illustration, not a required MoQ scheduling algorithm. It also does not measure capture-to-display latency: to measure that, we would need to relate the source's capture clock to the receiver's clock.

Audio and video need a shared synchronization strategy. For example, an audio sample and a video frame intended for media time 67 ms may arrive at different times. The player can hold the earlier one so both follow the same presentation clock. Their object arrival order is not enough. The player may have to buffer, wait, skip, or correct its presentation clock.

Group and object IDs are positions in the transport model, not substitutes for media timestamps. Keep those concepts separate even when an implementation happens to relate them.

## Build around the whole browser

A working media page must also handle capture permission, autoplay policy, device changes, tab lifecycle, and cleanup. Start playback from a user action when required, and make failures understandable.

The moq.dev stack provides higher-level player and publisher packages that handle much of this integration. For a first application, learn the lower layers conceptually while using the existing player. Reimplementing capture, clocks, and rendering at once makes transport debugging unnecessarily difficult.
